title: Why is "don't over-engineer" a core LLD skill (avoid forcing patterns, avoid a God class, start simple and refactor), and how do you answer the common follow-up "how would you extend this?" using the Open/Closed Principle (add a new class, not modify existing code)?
shortTitle: Why "don't over-engineer" is a core LLD skill, and answering "how would you extend this?" with the Open/Closed Principle
keyPoints: Over-engineering shows up as forced patterns, God classes, speculative generality, and premature abstraction.
Start simple and refactor: write the cohesive model first, apply a pattern when a real pressure appears.
A God class violates SRP by doing many unrelated things, becoming a merge-conflict magnet.
Answer "how would you extend this?" with OCP: add a new class implementing the existing interface, never modify tested code.
Balance: do not pre-build abstractions for every axis of change – place a seam only where change is genuinely likely.
Untouched code does not need re-testing and cannot regress, which is critical in banking systems.

s1_definition.oneliner: Build the simplest correct design and refactor when needed, then extend by adding a new class rather than modifying existing code, which is the Open/Closed Principle.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Not over-engineering** – building the simplest design that correctly satisfies current requirements, avoiding speculative abstractions and forced patterns.
- **God class** – a class that does too many things and changes for too many reasons; it violates SRP and is a merge-conflict magnet.
- **Start simple, refactor** – introduce a pattern only when a real need appears: a second implementation, a growing switch, a hard-to-test dependency.
- **Open/Closed Principle** – new behaviour is added by writing a new class that plugs into an existing abstraction, not by editing existing, tested code.
- **Seam** – a small interface placed where change is likely, so extension is easy without pre-building for every possible future.
s1_definition.analogy: Suppose National Bank of India asks Rajesh to design a system that today supports exactly one kind of fee. Over-engineering is building a configurable rule engine, a plugin framework, and a message bus for that single fee: a mansion when a room was asked for. The skilled move is to build the simple room cleanly and leave an obvious doorway for a future room. Then when Pankaj asks "what if we add a second fee type next year?", Rajesh answers: because I kept the fee behind a small interface, I just add one new class and never touch the existing fee code.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Over-Engineering vs Just Enough Design
  ───────────────────────────────────────

  OVER-ENGINEERED (one fee):
  ┌──────────────┐   ┌───────────────┐   ┌──────────────────┐
  │ FeeCalculator│──▶│ FeeFactory    │──▶│FlatFeeCalculator │
  │ (interface)  │   │ (factory)     │   │(only impl)       │
  └──────────────┘   └───────────────┘   └──────────────────┘
  Three files, one fee. Waste.

  JUST ENOUGH (one fee):
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ FeeService                   │
  │ FLAT_FEE = 50.00             │
  │ calculateFee(amount) → 50.00 │
  └──────────────────────────────┘
  One file. Done.

  JUST ENOUGH (when second fee arrives):
  ┌──────────────┐
  │ FeeStrategy  │ ◄── interface (seam added now)
  └──────┬───────┘
         ├── FlatFee
         └── PercentageFee (new – no edits to FlatFee)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Not over-engineering is the discipline of building the simplest design that correctly meets today's requirements, and it is a core low-level design skill because interviewers judge whether Rajesh knows when not to use a pattern just as much as whether he knows the patterns. Over-engineering shows up as forced patterns where a plain method would do, as a God class that does too many things and changes for too many reasons, as speculative generality built for an imagined future, and as premature abstraction introduced before any real variation exists.

Rajesh's approach at National Bank of India is to start simple and refactor. He writes the cohesive, straightforward model first, keeps each class to a single responsibility, and introduces a pattern only when a real pressure appears: a second variant, a growing switch statement, or a hard-to-test dependency.

The common follow-up is "how would you extend this?" and Rajesh answers it with the Open/Closed Principle: new behaviour is added by writing a new class that plugs into an existing abstraction, not by editing existing, working code. When Pankaj asks how to add a new fee type, Rajesh adds a new class implementing the existing interface and registers it, touching none of the existing classes. That reduces risk because untouched code cannot regress.

The judgment that ties it together is balancing simplicity and extensibility. Rajesh does not pre-build abstractions for every possible future, but he identifies the one or two axes where change is genuinely likely and places a small interface only along those axes. In his notification project he kept the service thin with a single SMS channel and placed one seam, a channel interface. When email and push were later needed, each was a new class with zero edits.

Remember one sentence: start with the simplest correct design, place a seam only where change is genuinely likely, and extend by adding a class, never by editing.
